learningObjective: Implement the circuit breaker pattern to prevent cascading failures in synchronous microservice communication during dependency degradation.

question: A company is migrating a fleet of 200 on-premises Windows and Linux servers to AWS. The servers run various workloads including web applications, batch processing jobs, and internal tools. The company wants to perform a lift-and-shift migration with minimal application changes. The migration team needs to discover and inventory all servers, track migration progress, and perform the actual server replication. The company wants to minimize downtime during the cutover — ideally under 1 hour per server. Which combination of AWS services should the solutions architect use for the migration? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Use AWS Application Discovery Service to discover on-premises servers, collect configuration data, and map dependencies between servers.
options.B: Use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) to continuously replicate server volumes to AWS and perform automated cutover with minimal downtime.
options.C: Use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) to replicate all server data, including operating systems and applications, to EC2 instances.
options.D: Create AMIs of each on-premises server using the VM Import/Export service and launch EC2 instances from the imported AMIs.
options.E: Use AWS Server Migration Service (SMS) to take periodic snapshots of on-premises VMs and replicate them to AWS.

explanation: A is correct because AWS Application Discovery Service automates the discovery and inventory of on-premises servers, collecting data including server specifications (CPU, memory, disk, network), installed software, running processes, and network connections between servers. This data enables the migration team to understand the server fleet, identify dependencies (which servers communicate with each other), and plan migration waves — grouping interdependent servers for coordinated migration. Discovery Service integrates with AWS Migration Hub, which provides a centralized dashboard to track the migration progress of all 200 servers. B is correct because AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is the primary AWS service for lift-and-shift server migration. MGN installs a lightweight replication agent on each source server that continuously replicates server volumes (OS, applications, data) to AWS in real-time using block-level replication. Because replication is continuous, the target servers in AWS are always nearly synchronized with the source. During cutover, MGN launches EC2 instances from the replicated data, applies necessary driver and network changes, and the server is running on AWS — typically with less than 1 hour of downtime (often minutes). MGN supports both Windows and Linux servers and handles the conversion from physical/virtual to EC2 automatically.

whyOthersAreWrong.C: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is designed specifically for database migration — it replicates database schemas and data between database engines (e.g., Oracle to Aurora, SQL Server to RDS). DMS does not replicate operating systems, applications, or server configurations. It cannot be used to migrate entire servers (OS + applications + data) to EC2 instances. DMS is the right tool for database migration, which may be part of the overall migration strategy, but it does not replace MGN for server migration.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: VM Import/Export can import virtual machine images (VMDKs, VHDs, OVAs) as AMIs, but it requires creating full VM exports from the on-premises hypervisor for each server. For 200 servers, exporting, uploading, and importing VM images is time-consuming and creates a significant downtime window — the VM must be exported (potentially requiring shutdown), uploaded to S3 (10s to 100s of GB per server), and imported as an AMI. Any data changes during this process are not captured, unlike MGN's continuous replication. VM Import/Export is a one-time snapshot approach without continuous synchronization, making the cutover window much larger than MGN's sub-1-hour target.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: AWS Server Migration Service (SMS) has been superseded by AWS Application Migration Service (MGN). AWS recommends MGN for all new migrations. SMS used incremental VM snapshot replication, which captures changes periodically (every 1-24 hours) rather than continuously. This periodic approach results in data that can be hours behind the source during cutover, potentially requiring longer downtime to capture final changes. MGN's continuous block-level replication provides near-real-time synchronization, enabling shorter cutover windows. SMS is in maintenance mode and lacks the features and performance of MGN.

learningObjective: Plan a large-scale server migration using Application Discovery Service for inventory and Application Migration Service for continuous replication with minimal-downtime cutover.

question: A company manages a fleet of IoT devices deployed in remote locations with intermittent internet connectivity. Each device generates JSON telemetry data (temperature, pressure, vibration readings) every 10 seconds. The company needs to process the telemetry data locally on the device for real-time anomaly detection (e.g., detecting when vibration exceeds a threshold) and trigger local alerts even when the device has no internet connectivity. When connectivity is available, the telemetry data must be forwarded to AWS IoT Core for centralized analytics. The company also needs to deploy and update the local processing logic remotely without physically accessing the devices. Which AWS service enables local data processing on IoT devices with cloud connectivity?

options.A: AWS IoT Greengrass deployed on each IoT device. Run Lambda functions locally on the device for anomaly detection. Use Greengrass MQTT messaging for local alerts and sync data to IoT Core when connectivity is available.
options.B: AWS IoT Core with device shadows to cache telemetry data locally. Use IoT Core rules to process data and detect anomalies in the cloud.
options.C: Deploy a lightweight Docker container on each device running custom anomaly detection code. Use AWS Systems Manager to manage and update the containers remotely.
options.D: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with the Kinesis Producer Library on each device to buffer telemetry data locally and stream it to AWS when connectivity is restored.

explanation: A is correct because AWS IoT Greengrass extends AWS cloud capabilities to edge devices, enabling local compute, messaging, data caching, and ML inference. Greengrass Core software runs on the IoT device and provides a local Lambda runtime — Lambda functions deployed to the device execute locally, processing telemetry data for anomaly detection without requiring internet connectivity. When vibration exceeds the threshold, the local Lambda function can trigger immediate alerts (activating local actuators, sending local MQTT messages, or writing to local displays). Greengrass manages local MQTT messaging between device components, enabling real-time local communication. When internet connectivity is available, Greengrass automatically synchronizes data with AWS IoT Core through its built-in store-and-forward capability — telemetry data is buffered locally during disconnection and forwarded when connectivity is restored. Greengrass deployments allow the company to remotely deploy and update Lambda functions, ML models, and configuration to devices from the AWS cloud console, eliminating the need for physical device access.

whyOthersAreWrong.B: AWS IoT Core device shadows maintain a JSON document representing the device's state (reported and desired), enabling the cloud to interact with devices even when they are offline. However, device shadows do not provide local data processing — all telemetry processing occurs in the cloud via IoT Core rules. When the device has no internet connectivity, no anomaly detection runs because IoT Core rules execute in the cloud. Device shadows are designed for state synchronization, not local compute. The requirement for real-time anomaly detection during disconnected periods cannot be met by a cloud-only processing approach.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Deploying Docker containers on devices can provide local processing, but AWS Systems Manager is designed for managing EC2 instances and on-premises servers, not lightweight IoT devices. Systems Manager requires the SSM agent, which is designed for server operating systems (Linux, Windows), not the embedded operating systems commonly used on IoT devices. Additionally, this approach requires building a custom deployment pipeline, update mechanism, and connectivity management framework. IoT Greengrass provides all of these capabilities as a managed service with purpose-built IoT device support, OTA (over-the-air) updates, and cloud integration.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: The Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) buffers records and sends them to Kinesis Data Streams, but it does not provide local data processing for anomaly detection. KPL is a data ingestion library — it collects, batches, and transmits data to the cloud. During disconnected periods, KPL would buffer data but cannot process it locally for anomaly detection or trigger alerts. The KPL is also a relatively heavy library designed for server-grade environments, not resource-constrained IoT devices. Kinesis Data Streams processes data in the cloud, which is not available during connectivity loss.

learningObjective: Deploy edge computing on IoT devices using AWS IoT Greengrass for local processing with intermittent cloud connectivity.

question: A company is building a content management system that stores documents in Amazon S3. The system must support the following access patterns: (1) content editors upload and manage documents through a web application, (2) external partners access specific shared folders via pre-signed URLs, (3) an internal analytics pipeline reads all documents for indexing, and (4) a compliance system must be notified whenever a document is created, modified, or deleted. The company also needs an event-driven trigger when specific file types (PDFs) are uploaded to a particular S3 prefix. Which combination of S3 features should the solutions architect configure to meet all access and notification requirements? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Configure S3 bucket policies with condition keys to grant content editors access via the web application's IAM role and restrict partner access to specific S3 prefixes.
options.B: Enable Amazon S3 Event Notifications with a filter for the PDF prefix and .pdf suffix, targeting a Lambda function for PDF-specific processing.
options.C: Enable Amazon EventBridge integration on the S3 bucket to send all object-level events (Created, Removed, Restored) to EventBridge, where rules route events to the compliance notification system.
options.D: Configure S3 Access Points — one for the web application with full read/write access and one for the analytics pipeline with read-only access — to simplify access management.
options.E: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to speed up document uploads from content editors and external partners.

explanation: B is correct because S3 Event Notifications with prefix and suffix filters enable targeted event-driven processing. Configuring a notification with a prefix filter (e.g., documents/pdfs/) and a suffix filter (.pdf) triggers a Lambda function only when PDF files are uploaded to the specific prefix, avoiding unnecessary invocations for other file types. This addresses the requirement for PDF-specific processing triggered by uploads to a particular prefix. C is correct because Amazon EventBridge integration with S3 provides comprehensive event routing for all object-level events. When enabled, S3 sends all object events (s3:ObjectCreated:*, s3:ObjectRemoved:*, etc.) to EventBridge, where rules can match specific events and route them to the compliance notification system. EventBridge provides advanced filtering, multiple targets per rule, and integration with dozens of AWS services. This gives the compliance system visibility into every document creation, modification, and deletion without modifying the application. EventBridge and S3 Event Notifications can coexist on the same bucket. D is correct because S3 Access Points simplify access management for different use cases on the same bucket. Each Access Point has its own endpoint, access policy, and network controls. The web application's Access Point can grant read/write access with specific IAM role conditions, while the analytics pipeline's Access Point can enforce read-only access. Access Points reduce the complexity of a single monolithic bucket policy and make it easier to manage permissions for different consumers. When new consumers are added, a new Access Point can be created without modifying existing policies.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: S3 bucket policies can implement access control, but managing multiple access patterns (content editors, partners, analytics pipeline) in a single bucket policy becomes complex and error-prone as the number of consumers grows. Each new access pattern requires modifying the central bucket policy, increasing the risk of misconfigurations that could grant excessive access or break existing access patterns. S3 Access Points (option D) provide a cleaner approach by giving each consumer its own isolated endpoint with independent access policies. Additionally, bucket policies alone do not address the event notification or PDF-specific processing requirements.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations to speed up uploads from geographically distant clients. While it can improve upload speeds, neither the content editors nor external partners are described as experiencing upload latency issues. Transfer Acceleration adds per-GB transfer costs and does not address any of the core requirements: access control, event notifications, or event-driven processing. It is a performance optimization feature that would only be justified if users are uploading from distant geographic locations and experiencing slow upload speeds.

learningObjective: Configure S3 Event Notifications, EventBridge integration, and Access Points to support diverse access patterns and event-driven workflows.
